detail:
Mayo Clinic's Q&A on POTS explains that patients often have low blood volume and describes increased fluids and sodium as a first-line measure: "Extra fluid is needed to fill up the vessels. … Drinking extra fluids alone isn't enough. Increased salt intake is also necessary to hold fluid in the blood vessels." The amount of salt and fluid recommended differs between sources — Cleveland Clinic's guidance is 2–3 L of water per day and 10–12 g of salt per day, while Dysautonomia International suggests 2–3 L of fluids and 3,000–10,000 mg of salt per day. Because of this range, the appropriate target is an individual decision for a clinician.

BMJ Best Practice cautions that increased salt intake is not appropriate for people with hypertension, kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease, and that adding salt should be done under physician supervision. Mayo Clinic's Q&A additionally recommends avoiding caffeine and alcohol.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor before changing fluid or salt intake.

summary: Sources describe increased fluid and sodium intake as a first-line approach for POTS, because many patients have low blood volume — but amounts differ by source and salt increases need physician supervision.
takeaways: Mayo Clinic describes extra fluid as needed to fill the vessels, adding that drinking extra fluids alone is not enough: increased salt intake is also necessary to hold fluid in the blood vessels.
Cleveland Clinic's stated guidance: 2–3 liters of water per day and 10–12 g of salt per day.
Dysautonomia International suggests 2–3 liters of fluids and 3,000–10,000 mg of salt per day — the ranges differ by source, so ask your doctor which applies to you.

Safety notes: BMJ Best Practice says high salt intake is inappropriate with hypertension, kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease, and Mayo's Q&A additionally recommends avoiding caffeine and alcohol. Talk to your doctor before increasing salt.
title: Extra fluids and salt for blood volume
